The weak therefore risk being swallowed by the strong. Their only security is to remain in balance with the others, with equal pressure on every side and political resistance.

We can see, then, that a state should sometimes widen its boundaries and sometimes limit them. One of the chief skills of civil policy is to tell these cases apart and set the proportion most helpful to preserving the state. As a general rule, reasons for expansion concern external and relative matters, and must yield to reasons for contraction, which concern internal and absolute matters. A sound, vigorous constitution comes first. A good government deserves far more trust than the resources an extensive territory might supply within the country’s own political life in civic life.

This is not to deny that some states have been formed so that conquest was essential to their very constitution. They may even have congratulated themselves on this fortunate necessity, which nevertheless marked, at the height of their greatness, the unavoidable moment of their fall.

chapters.title: Book II. CHAP. X. The subject continued.
paragraphs: A political body can be measured in two ways: by the land it covers and by the number of people who live there. Its true size depends on a suitable proportion between the two. The people make the state, while the land supports the people. The balance is right when the territory can sustain its inhabitants and the population is as large as that land can support. This proportion gives a given number of people their greatest strength. If the territory is too broad, defending it becomes costly, too little of it is cultivated, and its harvest exceeds what is needed; these are immediate reasons for defensive war. If the country is too small, the state must depend on its neighbours for some of its necessities; this directly invites offensive war. A people whose position leaves them no choice except trade or war will necessarily be weak: they rely on neighbours and uncertain events, and their existence can only be brief and precarious. They must either conquer others and change their circumstances, or be conquered and disappear. Such a state can keep its independence only by being too insignificant to threaten anyone or too powerful to be subdued.

It is difficult to calculate the exact balance between the amount of land and the population it can support. Soil varies in quality, fertility, and what it produces; climate also matters. The people differ just as much in their habits and physical needs: some consume little on fertile ground, while others need a great deal from barren land. We must also consider how readily women bear children, what circumstances increase or reduce population, and how many newcomers the legislator might attract through the benefits offered by his government. He should therefore judge not by the population now present but by what he can foresee in the future—not by today’s number but by the growth that will naturally follow. A thousand local conditions may allow a state to hold more land than it seems to need at present. A people might spread across a wide mountainous region, where forests and pastures take less work than cultivated fields; experience also tells us that women have more children there than on level ground. A large sloping surface may have only a small horizontal base, and it is by that base alone that we should estimate how much land can grow crops. By contrast, a people may live in a much smaller area along the sea, or among rocks and nearly barren sand, because fishing supplies their food in place of agriculture. They can also relieve their community of excess population by sending out colonies. Finally, they need to live close together to repel pirate attacks.

To the conditions already mentioned for establishing a people, we must add one that nothing else can supply and without which every other condition is pointless: they must have peace and plenty. The period when a state is being formed is like the time when soldiers are first arranged into a battalion: they are then least able to resist and easiest to defeat. Afterward, even when in complete disorder, they would resist more strongly than during that first unsettled moment, when each person is more occupied with his own place than with the shared danger. If war, famine, or rebellion broke out at this critical stage, the state would certainly be overthrown.

Many governments, it is true, have been set up during disorder and confusion. But in those instances the new governments themselves destroyed the state. Usurpers have always caused or exploited periods of widespread upheaval to secure ruinous laws that the people could never have been persuaded to accept in calmer times. Choosing the right moment to establish laws is one of the surest ways to tell a legislator’s purpose from a tyrant’s.

If we ask which people are ready to receive a system of laws, I would answer: those already joined by some original bond of interest or agreement, yet not truly subject to regular laws; those whose customs and prejudices have not taken deep root; those who need not fear being suddenly swallowed by an invasion and who can meet each neighbour separately without joining their quarrels, or call on one to help resist another. They should be people whose members know one another, among whom no one has to be burdened beyond what he can bear; who can survive without other nations and whose absence no other nation could not survive. They should be neither wealthy nor destitute, but self-sufficient. In a word, they should combine the steadiness of an old nation with the readiness to learn of a new one. The hardest part of legislation is less knowing what to establish than knowing what to remove. Its rare failures also reflect how impossible it is to find nature’s simplicity within society’s many demands. These conditions seldom come together, which is why so few states have much to praise in their constitutions. There is still one European country fit to receive laws: the island of Corsica. The bravery and determination with which its people won back and defended their liberty should inspire some wise person to teach them how to preserve it. I cannot help thinking that this small island may one day astonish Europe.

If two neighbouring peoples were placed so that one could not survive without the other, the first would be in a very harsh position and the second in great danger. Any wise nation in that position would free itself from the dependence as quickly as possible. The republic of Tlaxcala, in the middle of the Mexican empire, preferred to go without salt rather than buy it from the Mexicans or accept it as a gift. Its prudent citizens saw through the trap concealed in such generosity. That is how they kept their freedom. This little state, surrounded by the vast empire, ultimately helped bring about its downfall.

chapters.title: Book II. CHAP. XI. Of the various systems of legislature.
paragraphs: If we ask what the greatest good consists of, or what every system of lawmaking should aim to achieve, the answer comes down to two main ends: liberty and equality. Liberty is needed because every dependence on a private person drains strength from the state as a whole; equality is needed because liberty cannot survive without it.

I have already explained what social liberty is. Equality does not mean that everyone must have exactly the same wealth or power. It means that power must never be used against good order and law, and that no citizen should be rich enough to buy another or so poor that he must sell himself. This requires restraint in the wealth and influence of the great, and restraint in the wants and greed of those with less Such restraint also limits the dependence that unequal wealth creates.

If you want to give a state strength and stability, keep the two extremes as far apart as possible: let there be neither rich people nor beggars. These conditions go together, and both damage the commonwealth. One creates tyrants, the other those who support tyranny. Through them public liberty is traded: some buy it and others sell it.

People say this kind of equality is only an abstract fantasy and cannot be put into practice. But even if abuses cannot be avoided, does that mean we should not correct them? Things continually work against equality; for that very reason, laws should be designed to protect it.

These general aims of legislation must be adjusted to each country’s location, the character of its people, and the other circumstances that call for a distinct system of laws. The best system in theory may not be the one best suited to a particular state. If, for example, the soil is barren or the country too small for its population, encourage crafts and industry, whose products can be traded for what the people need. But if there are fertile hills and productive valleys, a rich soil and too few inhabitants, turn to farming, which supports population, and drive out destructive arts that gather the few people into one or two places and leave the rest of the country empty. If your country has a broad, convenient coastline, fill the sea with ships and cultivate navigation and trade; these may bring a brilliant but brief period of prosperity. If instead the waves break their force against your inaccessible cliffs, remain uncultivated and unlearned; perhaps you will live more comfortably, more virtuously, and certainly more happily. Beyond principles shared by all nations, each people has its own particular influence that makes its own laws suitable to itself alone. In ancient times among the Hebrews, and in more recent times among the Arabs, religion was the main concern of the nation; for Athens it was learning, for Carthage and Tyre commerce, for Rhodes seafaring, for Sparta war, and for Rome public virtue. The author of *The Spirit of Laws* has shown through many examples how a lawgiver should shape a system to serve each of these ends.

The Marquis d’A. says that the benefit of foreign trade is an illusion for the kingdom as a whole. It may enrich a few people, and perhaps some cities, but the nation gains nothing and the people are no better off.

A state’s constitution becomes truly solid and lasting when its natural and social relations agree. Then legislation works with nature, and laws merely confirm and, as it were, correct what nature dictates. But if the legislator misunderstands his aim and chooses a principle at odds with the nature of things—if law directs people towards slavery while nature favours freedom, towards riches while nature supports population, or towards peace while nature leads to war and conquest—the laws will gradually lose their force. The constitution will change, and the state will remain unsettled until it is wholly transformed or destroyed and nature has taken control again.
